units.spoken: RL Basics
No labels, just a reward after each try. How a learner gets better by trial and error.
Section one, Learning from rewards
Many tasks give no labelled answers, only a reward after each try. How can a learner get better from those rewards alone?
The running example is my banana collector, built in the Unity game engine, a learner in a square arena that should gather yellow bananas and avoid blue ones.
Reinforcement learning
Picture a learner with no right answers, only a number after each try. Learning from rewards like this is called reinforcement learning, or RL for short.
How. The learner tries a move, hears how good the result was, and tries again, and each try teaches it a little.
When it works, the learner finds good moves without ever being shown one.

Take a look at this figure. The whole problem sits in one square room. The collector sees only numbers, picks one of four moves, and hears a single number back, plus one for a yellow banana and minus one for a blue one. Nothing tells it which move was right. That is the whole of reinforcement learning: a learner that gets better by trial and error, with no teacher and no right answers, only the pay after each try.
Figure 1 shows the arena the whole page keeps coming back to. The yellows are the bananas to gather, the blues are the ones to avoid, and their pay is all the agent ever hears.
Once trained, the collector gathers yellows quickly and steps around blues.
Section two, The reinforcement learning loop

Here the agent is the banana collector, the learner that picks the moves. It is paid for each yellow banana it eats and charged for each blue one, but it is not told in advance which steps pay; it finds out only by stepping. A state is the agent’s situation right now. A move, or action, is one choice the agent can make in a state, and a reward is the number the world hands back after each move, good or bad.

In the arena most steps meet no banana, so most steps bring no reward at all. The collector may always pick the same move or pick by chance. The collector sees the bananas around it and must decide which way to step from each spot.

The world can be random too, so the same move in the same state does not always lead to the same next state or reward. New bananas drop in new places, so the collector’s path changes from one run to the next.
Moves go down, rewards come back
Picture the collector on one spot, choosing a step, and the world answering. The environment is everything outside the agent that responds and hands back a reward.
How. The policy, the agent’s rule for choosing a move in each state, picks a move. The world applies it and hands back a reward and the next state, and the agent learns from each reward.
When it works, each step leaves the agent a little surer of which way to step from each spot.

Take a look at this figure. Every step runs the same loop. The agent sees the state, picks a move, and the world answers with a reward and a new state. The loop never changes; what changes is what the agent does inside it. Learning is the loop running again and again, each time with a slightly better rule for picking the move.

Figure 2 shows the loop the agent repeats for its whole training, one move answered by a reward and a next state. The move goes down to the world, and the reward and the next state come back up, so the two arrows matter more than the two boxes.
Section three, The banana collector environment
The collector sees only its sensors
Picture a small square room the collector sees only through its sensors. An episode is one run from the start until it ends, and a discrete action is one move from a fixed short list.
How. The collector reads the arena through a list of sensor readings, one list per step, and chooses from only four moves.
When it works, that tiny pay, a gain for a yellow banana and a loss for a blue one, is enough to turn guessing into good play.
The arena's clock ends the run.
The collector sees the arena only through 37 sensor readings and chooses from only four moves, so every score on this page is about those readings and those moves.
The loop in code starts with a policy that picks every move by chance.
This code opens the banana arena and starts a run, with the collector ready to move.
This code draws the next move by chance, one of the four moves, picked at random.
This code sends the move to the arena and reads back what happened: the new state, the reward, and whether the run ended.

The snippet follows the Value-based-methods repo’s pinned versions, the unityagents package with Python 3.6; the ML-Agents Toolkit, the Unity toolkit the snippet is written against, has since changed its API.

sections.section: 4 Why copying an expert is not enough

units.spoken: Section four, Why copying an expert is not enough
Behaviour cloning
Picture an expert’s recorded routes through the arena, and a learner copying them. Behaviour cloning is copying an expert’s recorded moves as labels and training on them.
How. The expert’s recordings show only a few routes through the arena, and the rest of it stays unseen, so the collector has only its rewards to learn from.
When copying works, it needs a recorded right answer for every step, and this arena has none.

Language models are first trained this way, by copying example replies, before reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) improves them, as Aligning Language Models with RL shows. In the arena the collector learns from its rewards alone.

Take a look at this figure. Copying an expert works only where the expert has been. The expert shows the right move, and the learner copies it, but on a spot the expert never visited there is nothing to copy. Reinforcement learning hears only how good the result was, so it can learn on spots no expert ever visited, but it has to discover the good moves itself, one try at a time.
Figure 3 shows the two ways to learn side by side. The top half needs labels the arena never had; the bottom half is all the collector gets, a reward after each try.
Section five, Why RL is hard
A yellow banana sits in the open while another hides behind a blue one, so the collector must choose which to head for first.
Later bananas count for less
Picture the collector choosing between a yellow banana one step away and a better route three steps on. The return is all the reward still to come, with later rewards counted a little less.
How. Each later reward is shrunk by the discount, the share of a reward’s worth kept for each step of delay, so nearer bananas count more.
When it works, the collector heads for the route that pays most over the whole run, not just the next banana.

Take a look at this figure. The discount is the price of waiting: a banana now is worth more than the same banana later. That single idea makes the agent prefer sooner rewards, and it turns a whole run of rewards into one number the agent can compare.
Figure 4 shows why a reward that arrives later is worth less than one that arrives now. The bars under the steps fade the further ahead they are.
Equation 1. The collector has to choose between a banana now and a better route later. A delivery robot choosing between a quick drop-off now and a fuller route later faces the same choice.
Take a look at this equation. It scores a whole run by adding up the rewards still to come, each shrunk by the discount.

The return line. G sub t is the return from step t. The return is the rewards still to come, added up. R sub t plus one is the reward right after the move. Gamma is the discount, the share kept per step of delay. R sub t plus two is the reward one step further on. The plus sign adds the next reward to the discounted one after it. Intuitively, the return is the rewards still to come, each shrunk by delay.

Intuition. The return is one number for a whole run: plus for each yellow banana eaten, minus for each blue one, with nearer bananas counting more. This line starts the sum with the first two rewards.
Example. Take a run where the collector eats a yellow banana now and another one step later: the later banana counts less, shrunk once for each step of delay.

The continuing sum line. Gamma squared is the discount applied twice, once per step of delay. R sub t plus three is the reward three steps on. The plus sign adds it to the sum, and the dots mean more terms follow.
Intuitively, the sum runs on, each reward shrunk once more per step.
Example. Take a run that earns bananas at the first, third, and last steps: each later banana joins the sum shrunk once more per step of delay.

The whole sum line. G sub t is the return from step t. The sum over k adds up the rewards over every step of delay. K counts steps of delay, so zero is the next reward. Gamma to the k is the discount applied k times. R sub t plus k plus one is the k-plus-1 reward. The line says the return equals the sum of each reward times its discount. Intuitively, the whole sum fits in one line, every reward shrunk by delay.
termList: r sub t plus k plus one

units.spoken: Intuition. It is the sum built up reward by reward: the first at full worth, the next shrunk once, the next shrunk twice, and so on to the end of the episode.
Example. Take a run that earns a banana at every step: the sum adds them all, each shrunk once more than the one before, and k counts how many steps of delay each one carries.

The one-step line. G sub t is the return from step t. R sub t plus one is the reward right after the move. Gamma is the discount, the share kept per step of delay. G sub t plus one is the return from the next step. It holds the same later rewards, each with one fewer discount applied. The line says the return is the next reward plus the discounted return after it.
Intuitively, the return is the next reward plus the return after it.
Example. Take a run with no banana for three steps, then a yellow one: the return from the first spot is just that later banana, shrunk once per step.

Take the collector standing one step from a yellow banana, with a blue banana just past it. The return from that spot counts the yellow banana it is about to eat at full worth, then the blue banana after it shrunk once by the discount, then every banana after that shrunk once more per step, until the clock ends the episode.

What this figure is teaching is that the discount sets how far ahead the agent cares. With a big discount the bars stay tall far out, so rewards many steps away still count; with a small discount they fade fast, so only the next few steps matter. The same run scores differently under different discounts, and the discount is the knob that sets how patient the agent is.

Try the small, middle and large buttons and watch the bars. A bigger discount keeps far rewards counting, so the bars stay tall far out; a smaller one fades them fast. The same rewards score differently at each setting, and the discount is the knob that sets how patient the agent is.

Figure 5 shows the discount from Equation 1 at work, how a reward loses worth with every step of delay. The three buttons set the discount to small, middle, or large, and the bars redraw, shrinking from left to right as the delay grows. The tool opens on the middle setting, a discount of 0.8. Raising it toward 0.95 keeps the bars tall for longer; lowering it toward 0.5 makes them fade fast.

Credit assignment is working out which earlier moves earned a reward that arrives much later. In the arena a yellow banana can be eaten many steps after the turn that led to it, and that turn still deserves the credit.

sections.section: 6 Scoring states and moves with values

units.spoken: Section six, Scoring states and moves with values
Six point one, What a spot and a move are worth
Spots and moves have scores
Picture the arena floor shaded by how good each spot is. A spot is worth the return to expect from standing on it, and a move is worth the return to expect after making it.
How. An expected value is the average over everything that can happen by chance, weighted by how likely each outcome is, so the score already allows for luck.
When it works, the collector can compare spots and moves before it moves, and head for the spots worth most.

Take a look at this figure. A spot is worth what the runs from it earn, so the price of a spot rises near a yellow banana and falls near a blue one. The value is a price on a spot, learned from experience, and once every spot has a price the agent can compare spots before it moves. The best move is the one that leads to the best-priced spot.

Figure 6 shows what a state's value looks like on the floor: darker spots are worth more. The dark corner sits beside the yellows and the pale corner beside the blues, so the shading is the collector's whole knowledge about where to stand.
Equation 2. Once the return scores a whole run, the agent needs to compare spots and moves before it moves. A warehouse robot that must pick which aisle to enter next needs the same scores.
Take a look at this equation. It scores a spot and a move by the runs they lead to, on average.

The spot value line. V pi of s is the state value under the policy. Pi is the policy, the rule for choosing moves. E sub pi is the average over runs under that policy. G sub t is the return from step t. The bar reads given s sub t equals s. The value is the average return from this spot, over the runs the policy produces. Intuitively, a spot is worth what the runs from it earn on average.
Intuition. The move value scores a single move first, while this line averages over the moves the policy plays first.
Example. Take a spot one step from a yellow banana and two steps from a blue one: most runs from there earn the yellow first.

The move value line. Q pi of s and a is the move value. Pi is the policy, the rule for choosing moves. E sub pi is the average over runs under that policy. G sub t is the return from the move on. The bar reads given the step's spot is s and the move is a. The value is the average return after this move, over the runs that follow it.
termList: Q pi of s and a

units.spoken: Intuitively, a move is worth what the runs after it earn on average.
Example. Take a spot where two moves both reach a yellow banana, but one passes a blue one first: the safer move scores higher, while the spot's value averages both moves.

Take the collector on the spot one step from a yellow banana. Stepping toward it eats the banana on the next move, and the runs after that step branch from the spot past the banana, while stepping away leaves the banana for later runs, so the two moves carry different values even though they start from the same spot.
Before training, the agent has no idea which spots lie near yellows.

Best play is the goal of the whole page: the policy that earns the most return. Q star is each move’s value under that best policy, the score the learning is aiming at, not the score the agent already has. It is not Q pi, which scores moves under the policy the agent is following now, and nobody hands the collector that policy; it has to find it by stepping.
Six point two, Improving a guess after one step
The collector does not know the value for any spot, so it keeps a guess for each spot and improves it.

A guess needs something to aim at: a target, the value a guess is pulled toward. Monte Carlo, or MC for short, builds its target from the whole return. TD stands for temporal difference, the difference between two guesses a step apart, and one-step TD builds its target from one step's reward plus the guess for the next spot.
Targets and the one-step update
Picture the collector guessing how good each spot is, with nothing to aim at.
How. Each step brings a small surprise, the gap between the target and the guess, and each surprise moves a guess a little.
When it works, the guesses for spots near yellows end up higher than those near blues, and the surprise averages out to zero.

Here is the point of this figure. Two ways to aim a guess sit side by side. One waits for the run to end and uses the return the run really earned, exact for that run but slow to arrive. The other uses one step's reward plus the guess for the next spot, fast but leaning on a guess. The whole of this section is the trade between waiting for the truth and learning from a guess.

Figure 7 shows the two timelines side by side. The timelines differ in only one thing, when the update happens, and that difference is what lets one-step TD learn from every step instead of waiting for a run to end.
Equation 3. The agent's guesses need something to aim at. A self-driving car that must judge whether a turn was good needs the same choice.
Take a look at this equation. It names the two targets a guess can aim at.

The Monte Carlo target line. Y MC sub t is the Monte Carlo target at step t. MC stands for Monte Carlo, and t is the step. G sub t is the return from step t. The line says the target equals the return the run really earned.
Intuitively, the Monte Carlo target is the return the run really earned.
Example. Take a run where the collector eats two yellow bananas before the clock ends the episode: the Monte Carlo target is the full discounted score of that run.

The TD target line. Y TD sub t is the TD target at step t. TD means temporal difference, two guesses a step apart. R sub t plus one is the reward just seen. Gamma is the discount. V of s sub t plus one is the next spot's guess. The plus sign adds the discounted guess to the reward just seen.
termList: V of s sub t plus one

units.spoken: Intuitively, the TD target is a reward plus a guess for the next spot.
Example. Take a step where the collector eats nothing: the TD target is the discounted guess for the spot it lands on.

Take a step where the collector eats a yellow banana and lands one step from another. The TD target adds the yellow banana just eaten to the discounted guess for the spot it landed on. The two targets agree only when the guess for the new spot already matches what the runs from there really earn.
Equation 4. The agent now has targets to aim at and values to move. A chess program that updates its judgment of a position after each move follows the same rule.
Take a look at this equation. It says how a guess moves toward its target, step by step.

The true target line. Y pi sub t is the policy's target at step t. Pi on top marks the policy, the rule for choosing moves. R sub t plus one is the reward just seen. Gamma is the discount. V pi of s sub t plus one is the next value. The plus sign adds the discounted true value to the reward just seen. Intuitively, the true target is the reward plus the next spot's true value.
termList: V pi of s sub t plus one

units.spoken: Intuition. It is the TD target with true values in place of the agent's guesses.
Example. Take the collector stepping toward a yellow banana not yet reached: the target is the step's reward plus the true value of the spot it lands on.

The true value line. V pi of s sub t is this spot's true value. Pi on top marks the policy. E sub pi is the average over what can happen next. Y pi sub t is the true target for this step. The bar reads given s sub t. The value is the average of the true targets, each weighted by its chance. Intuitively, the true value is the average of the true targets.
termList: V pi of s sub t

units.spoken: Intuition. It averages the true target, one step's reward plus the true value of the next spot, the way the spot value averaged the return.
Example. Take a spot with two moves, one toward a yellow banana and one away: the true value averages both moves' targets by their chances.

The surprise line. Delta sub t is the TD error at step t. Y TD sub t is the TD target for this step. V of s sub t is the current guess for this spot. The line says the error is the target minus the guess. A positive error means the step went better than guessed, so the guess rises.
Intuitively, the surprise is the gap between the target and the guess.
Example. Take a step where the collector eats a yellow banana, with the guess for the spot rated low: the target beats the guess, so the surprise is positive.

The update line. V of s sub t on the left is the new guess. The arrow reads replace with. V of s sub t on the right is the old guess. Eta is the learning rate, the share the guess takes in. Delta sub t is the TD error, target minus guess. The line says the new guess is the old guess plus eta times the error.
Intuitively, each step moves the guess part of the way toward the target.
Example. Take a step where the collector eats a blue banana, with the guess for the spot rated highly: the guess falls part of the way.

Take the collector standing one step from a yellow banana with a low guess for that spot. It steps toward the banana and eats it, so the target comes out above the old guess, the surprise is positive, and the guess for the spot it stood on moves part of the way toward the target. Step after step, the guesses for the spots near the banana rise.

Each guess moves with a learning rate of 0.1 in this example, so each guess moves a tenth of its surprise per step. Raising the learning rate moves guesses further each step, faster but jumpier; lowering it moves them less, slower but steadier.
Section seven, Explore early, exploit late
If the agent keeps a score for every move, it faces a choice at every step: play the best-scored move or try one it knows less about. Equation 5 writes the rule that balances the two.
Explore and exploit
Picture the collector at a crossing, one move scored above the rest and the rest untried. Exploration means trying moves to learn what they do; exploitation means playing the best-scored move.
How. The balance is set by the explore share, called epsilon, the chance of a random move. The greedy move is the best-scored move, and it can hide a better route the agent never tried.
When it works, the collector tries enough new routes to find the yellows its best-scored move never turns toward, then settles on the best route it knows.

Equation 5. Values tell the agent which move scores best, but the best-scored move is only as good as the scores behind it, and untried moves have no scores at all. A streaming service choosing which film to recommend faces the same balance.
Take a look at this equation. It says when the agent plays its best-scored move and when it tries a random one.

The greedy line. A sub t is the move at step t. Argmax over a picks the move whose score is largest. Q of s sub t and a is the current move score. The line says the move played has the largest score. Intuitively, the greedy move is the best-scored move.
termList: Q of s sub t and a

units.spoken: Intuition. The agent plays it whenever it is not trying a random move, which is why it needs a random move alongside it, tried with chance epsilon, to find better routes.
Example. Take the collector at a crossing with one move scored above the rest: the greedy line plays that move.

The random line. A sub t is the move at step t. Epsilon is the explore share, the chance of a random move. Raising it tries more and uses what is known more slowly. Lowering it may never find a better route. The line says the move is drawn at random, with chance epsilon.
Intuitively, sometimes the collector ignores the scores and tries a random move.
Example. Take the collector on a spot where every move scores low: a random step can stumble on a yellow banana no move had scored.

Take the collector at a crossing where one move leads toward a yellow banana and the others lead away. It plays the best-scored move toward the banana, and once in a while it tries a move at random instead. That random step is how it can stumble on a banana it had never scored, and the scores it learns from the stumble are what the greedy move uses next time.

An agent can also shrink epsilon a little after every episode, so early on it mostly explores and late in training it mostly plays its best-scored move; Q-Learning, which learns a score for every move from one step at a time, shows the rule.
This code runs the epsilon-greedy rule: with chance epsilon it picks a random move, and otherwise it plays the best-scored move.

Exploring is easiest to watch on a small floor where every step can be seen. A warehouse robot looks for its charging dock; the ledge is the strip of floor between the start and the dock. It starts in one bottom corner and the dock sits in the other. Each move’s reward is minus the battery it uses, so the best total is the one closest to zero. Stepping onto the ledge costs a lot and puts the robot back at the start; only reaching the dock ends the episode. The cheapest way to the dock is the shortest path that never steps onto the ledge, and it runs right beside the ledge, so one random step there is a fall.

Take a look at this figure. Two robots learn by the same rule, and the difference is the explore share. One keeps a fixed epsilon, trying the same share of random moves all the way through. The other shrinks its epsilon each episode, exploring early and settling late. The fixed one keeps stumbling; the shrinking one finds the short route and stays on it. Exploring costs falls now and pays later, and shrinking the explore share is how the agent cashes in what it found.

Try setting the fixed robot's epsilon to a lot and pressing Play. Watch the two robots race for 200 episodes: the one that tries more random moves keeps falling, while the one that shrinks its epsilon settles on the short route. Then try a little and watch it settle faster, and ask what it might have missed by settling early.

Figure 8 shows two warehouse robots learning the same floor by the rule from Equation 5, one with a fixed epsilon and one whose epsilon shrinks each episode. The three buttons set the fixed robot's epsilon, opening on 0.1, and Play runs both robots for 200 episodes; each floor shows its robot's path, and the readout under it says whether it has settled or is still wandering. With the fixed epsilon set to a lot, the fixed robot still wanders and falls by the ledge, while the shrinking robot finds the short route and stays on it.

sections.section: 8 A learning step, start to finish

units.spoken: Section eight, A learning step, start to finish
These steps improve the guess of how good each spot is under the moves the agent is making now; choosing moves by learned move scores is the topic of Q-Learning.

Take a look at this figure. One learning step, broken into six moves. The agent sees its spot, picks a move, earns a reward, and lands somewhere new. Then it compares the target with its old guess and moves the guess part of the way toward the target. The six steps are the whole learning rule in miniature, and every step the agent ever takes runs this same shape.

Try stepping through the six steps with Next, or jump to a step with the numbered buttons. Watch the bar for the spot the agent stands on: at step 5 the marker appears beside it and the gap between them shades in, and at step 6 the bar moves part of the way to the marker. That move of the bar is the learning step itself, and every step the agent takes runs the same six moves.
Equation 6. The walkthrough in Figure 9 steps through one learning step in the arena. A warehouse robot that updates its judgment of one aisle after a single delivery faces the same step.
Take a look at this equation. It walks one learning step, from target to surprise to a better guess.

The target line. Y TD sub t is the target for this step. R sub t plus one is the reward the step just earned. Gamma is the discount. V of s sub t plus one is the lit bar's guess. The line says the target is the reward plus the discounted guess. Intuitively, the target is the reward plus the discounted guess.
termList: V of s sub t plus one

units.spoken: Intuition. The lit bar is the guess for the spot the agent landed on.
Example. Take the step the walkthrough shows: the collector eats a yellow banana, so the target is that banana's reward plus the discounted guess for the spot it lands on.

The surprise line. Delta sub t is the shaded gap, the target minus the guess. Y TD sub t is the TD target. V of s sub t is the guess for this spot. When the target sits past the bar the gap is positive and the guess rises. When it sits short of the bar, the gap is negative and the guess falls. Intuitively, the surprise is the gap between the target and the guess.
Intuition. At step 5 the marker appears beside the first bar and the gap between them shades in: the target minus the guess.
Example. Take a step where the collector eats a blue banana, with the guess for the spot rated highly: the target falls below the guess, so the surprise is negative.

The update line. V of s sub t on the left is the new guess. The arrow reads replace with. V of s sub t on the right is the old guess. Eta is the learning rate, the share the guess takes in. Delta sub t is the shaded gap, the target minus the guess. The bar moves by eta times the gap, so the new guess sits between the old guess and the marker. Intuitively, each step moves the guess part of the way toward the target.
Intuition. At step 6 the first bar moves part of the way to the marker, by a share of the gap, and the step runs again from the new guess.
Example. Take a step where the collector eats a blue banana: the surprise is negative, and the guess falls.
Take the step the walkthrough shows: the collector eats a yellow banana and lands on a spot whose guess is still low. The next time the collector stands on that spot, its guess is higher.

Figure 9 walks one learning update from start to finish in six steps, from a spot to a better guess of its value. Step 1 shows the agent in a state with its guess bar; step 2 has the policy pick a move; step 3 shows the world answering with reward and next state. Step 4 lights the target line, one step’s reward plus the discounted guess for the next spot, step 5 brings the target marker in, and step 6 moves the first bar toward it, the update that moves the guess by a share of the surprise. In the step shown, the collector eats a yellow banana and its guess moves part of the way toward the target.
Section nine, The trained banana agent

Take a look at this figure. After training, the behaviour looks sensible: the agent goes for the yellows and steers around the blues. Nobody wrote those rules. The curves came from the scores: spots near yellows priced high, spots near blues priced low, and the best-scored move at each spot drawing the path. The figure is what learning looks like when it is done.

Figure 10 shows the trained agent at work: its path bends around the blue bananas on its way to the yellows, showing the scores it learned, and at one bend it turns away from a blue banana right in its path and reaches the yellow behind it instead.
My trained agent learns a score for each move with a neural network, as in Deep Q-Networks (DQN). Over training the agent’s total reward per episode climbs as it learns to head for yellows.

The agent trains only every fourth move, on a small batch drawn from a large memory of past steps, so most moves are just play and only some are study. The memory matters because each step can be learned from more than once, and a batch drawn from many past runs is steadier than the last few steps alone. The learning rate, the discount and the explore share are the same three knobs the earlier sections introduced, though the trained agent sets them to its own values, and the move scores come from a network that takes 37 readings in and puts out 4 move values.
Section ten, Reward hacking

Reward hacking is when the agent earns the reward without doing what the designer meant. In the boat racing game CoastRunners, an OpenAI agent learned to circle and hit the same targets again and again instead of finishing the race.
The pay becomes the goal
Picture the collector paid for getting closer to a yellow banana, stepping closer, then away, then closer, without ever eating.
How. Reward shaping adds extra pay for progress toward the goal. The safe kind also takes the pay back when the agent moves away, so going round a loop earns no net bonus.
When it works, the pay the designer writes matches what the designer meant, and the agent cannot earn by looping.

A reward model is a network trained to score answers the way people would. A chat model trained against such a score can learn replies that please the score more than the people it stands for, as Aligning Language Models with RL shows.

The tool runs in a small practice arena with one yellow banana and a few blue ones; a banana does not come back once eaten, and a clock ends the episode. In this arena the designer pays a small bonus whenever a step brings the agent closer to the yellow banana.

Equation 7. The reward is the only pay the agent hears, so what the designer writes here decides what the agent learns. A delivery company that pays its drivers per delivery faces the same gap: pay for deliveries, and drivers rush; pay for careful driving, and they slow down.
Take a look at this equation. It writes the pay the agent hears, first as meant and then as shaped.

The meant pay line. R sub t plus one is the reward after the move. Yellow sub t plus one is one when a yellow is eaten. Blue sub t plus one is one when a blue is eaten. The minus sign takes the blue count off the yellow count. Intuitively, the meant pay is the yellow count minus the blue count.
Intuition. The shaped pay is this pay plus a bonus for progress.
Example. Take a step where the collector eats a yellow banana and no blue one: the meant pay counts that yellow and nothing else.

The shaped pay line. R shaped sub t plus one is the shaped reward. R sub t plus one is the meant pay. C is the bonus size, the pay per step closer. B sub t plus one is one for a step closer. The plus sign adds the progress bonus to the meant pay.
termList: r shaped sub t plus one

units.spoken: Intuitively, the shaped pay is the meant pay plus a bonus for progress.
Example. Take a step where the collector eats a yellow banana after stepping closer: the shaped pay counts the banana plus the bonus.

Take a step that brings the collector closer to the yellow banana without eating it. The meant pay is nothing, since no banana was eaten, but the shaped pay adds the progress bonus, so the agent is paid for progress even before it eats. That is the bonus a looping agent games: it can earn the bonus again and again by stepping closer, then away, then closer, without ever eating.

What this figure is teaching is that a careless reward teaches the wrong thing. The shaped pay adds a bonus for getting closer, so the agent finds a way to earn the bonus without ever eating: it loops back and forth, closer, then away, then closer again, paid each time for progress. The reward is the only instruction the agent hears, and a bonus for progress is an instruction to loop.

Try setting the bonus to none and pressing Play, then try large. With no bonus the agent eats bananas; with a large bonus it loops, earning the progress pay again and again without eating. Watch how the same arena teaches two different behaviours, and how the bonus, not the bananas, decides what the agent learns.

Figure 11 shows two agents in the same practice arena, one paid for bananas only and one paid a bonus for stepping closer to the yellow banana. The three buttons set the bonus from the shaped pay, the meant pay plus a bonus for progress, opening on the large bonus of 0.6, and Play runs both agents for 4,000 episodes. At the small bonus of 0.1 the shaped agent still eats the banana, while at the large bonus of 0.6 it steps in and back out beside the yellow banana without eating it, so the threshold lies between 0.1 and 0.6.

sections.section: 11 Scores, chances or one fixed output

units.spoken: Section eleven, Scores, chances or one fixed output

The collector acts on what it senses, not on the full state. What it senses at one moment is an observation: here, the arena’s sensor readings, which can be less than the full state. A spot with a blue banana just out of sight and a spot without one can give the collector the same readings.
Three ways a policy picks a move
Picture the banana agent on one spot, comparing its four move scores and playing the tallest bar. A policy can pick a move by scores, by chances, or by one fixed output.

How. A stochastic policy gives each move a chance and draws its move, instead of always playing the same move in the same state. A deterministic policy always plays the same move in the same state. Some agents output one amount every time instead of picking from a list of moves.
When it works, the shape fits the job: scores for the banana agent, chances for a chat model choosing its next word, one fixed output for a robot arm.
The trained banana agent compares move scores and plays the best-scored move. Equation 8 writes the draw down.

Here is the point of this figure. Three ways to turn numbers into a move. One picks the move with the tallest bar. One draws a move by lottery from the policy's chances. One always outputs the same thing. The choice shapes everything: whether the agent explores, whether it can surprise itself, and what it can learn. The trained banana agent picks the best-scored move, but the other two shapes are waiting in the next tutorials.

Figure 12 shows the three ways a policy can pick a move: by scores, by chances, or by one fixed output. Scores pick the tallest bar, chances draw one bar by lottery, and one fixed output is the same arrow every time.

Equation 8. The page has shown policies that pick the best-scored move and policies that sometimes pick at random. It leads to Policy Gradient Methods, which learn the policy itself. A chat model choosing its next word faces the same choice.
Take a look at this equation. It draws a move at random from the policy's chances.

The draw line. A is the move the agent makes. The drawn-from sign reads drawn at random from. Pi of a given s is the policy's chance for move a. Each move's chance depends on the spot. The line says the move is drawn at random from the policy's chances. Intuitively, this policy draws its move at random from its chances.
Intuition. The trained banana agent does not draw this way; it plays its best-scored move.
Example. Take a spot where the policy gives two moves equal chance: the draw picks either one, and the agent cannot be sure which it will play.

Take the collector on a spot where the policy gives one move most of the chance and the others a little each. Most draws pick the favored move, but now and then a draw picks another, which is how a policy of this shape explores without a separate random branch. A chat model choosing its next word works the same way: it gives every word a chance and draws one.
Section twelve, Choosing what to learn next
Which family of methods should you learn first, and what does each one learn?

Start with Q-Learning. The value methods learn how good each move is; the policy methods learn what to do; the model methods learn how the world works; and the multi-agent methods handle several learners on one floor.
